summary: Studies whether coding agents (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash via a GitHub Copilot SDK agent) write useful observability code. RQ1 strips logging/tracing from 1,223 functions in 10 open-source and 8 Microsoft-internal repositories and scores restoration by placement F1 and 'KeyBag' F1 over diagnostic variables; RQ2 generates 200 microservice systems from specs, deploys them on Kubernetes and injects 13 Chaos Mesh faults (1,615 fault instances per model) to measure how often logs expose fault-specific signals; RQ3 adds an observability skill distilled from ~200 internal incident commits.

claims.claim: Agents recover placement better than diagnostic content; explicit instructions cause over-generation
claims.evidence: Table II: blind prompt Position F1 0.551/0.580/0.278 vs KeyBag F1 0.357/0.294/0.237 (GPT-5.5/Opus 4.8/Gemini 3.5 Flash); hinted prompt raises statements 4.9 vs 2.1 but KeyBag precision 0.33->0.20, F1 0.36->0.26; few-shot raises KeyBag F1 0.357->0.383. Ground truth is human-written logging, which authors admit is not optimal. Differences of 0.02-0.04 F1 reported without spread despite '5 repeats'.

claims.claim: Generated systems expose fault signals for only 4.95%-13.99% of injected faults
claims.evidence: Table III and §IV-B; subset FSR up to 20.62% on successfully executed services; per-fault breakdown upstream failure 27.45% vs time skew 1.26%. FSR uses author-built fault-specific log oracles that may miss indirect signals (§V-B). Logs only; traces and metrics excluded.

claims.claim: An observability skill improves FSR, Position F1 and KeyBag F1, but gains are limited
claims.evidence: Table V / §IV-C: FSR GPT-5.5 4.95->13.62 (+8.67 pp), Opus 4.8 6.32->7.31 (+0.99 pp), Gemini 13.99->16.53 (+2.54 pp). No variance or significance; the +0.99 pp may be noise. Skill content only summarized at high level.

patterns.note: A domain skill helps observability metrics consistently but modestly; effect size varies 1-9 pp by model.
About observability of generated systems rather than harness tracing; shows functional runnability does not imply diagnosability.
Uses deployment plus fault injection as an execution-based oracle for a non-functional property.
Systems generated from 200 architecture specs that evidently did not specify observability; implies observability must be an explicit acceptance criterion.
Includes 8 industrial repositories (782 instances) in RQ1, though unreleased.

methodology.sample: RQ1: 1,223 instances (441 from 10 OSS microservice repos, 782 from 8 industrial repos); RQ2: 200 generated systems, 13 fault types, 1,615 fault instances per model; RQ3: same workloads with skill
methodology.baselines: Prompting variants (blind, hinted, few-shot) and skill vs no skill; no non-LLM baseline (e.g. log-insertion tools)
methodology.models: GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash through GitHub Copilot SDK
methodology.variance: Each experiment repeated five times and averaged; no standard deviations or CIs reported
methodology.contamination_controls: None stated; OSS repos (train-ticket, eShop, microservices-demo, etc.) are likely in training data, which would inflate RQ1 restoration
methodology.languages: Multi-language OSS repos (e.g. train-ticket Java, eShop .NET, NestJS TypeScript); per-language results and generated-system languages not reported in the sections read

standards.artifacts: §III-E 'Implementation and Reproducibility' lists models/harness; no release of generated systems, oracles, skill text or industrial data found

biases.detail: Five repeats claimed but only means shown; small deltas (e.g. +0.99 pp FSR) uninterpretable.
KeyBag F1 measures overlap with human logging, which authors concede is not an ideal reference; FSR depends on custom oracles.
Industrial repositories, incident commits behind the skill, and evaluation harness not released.
Popular OSS microservice demos used for restoration are likely memorized.
Gemini 3.5 Flash is worst on RQ1 restoration but best on RQ2 FSR; not explained, suggesting metric or setup sensitivity.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: GitHub Copilot SDK (Microsoft-owned) used as harness; OpenAI, Anthropic, Google models evaluated; findings are negative for all
coi.detail: Vendor-affiliated authors, but the paper does not promote a Microsoft product; Copilot SDK is infrastructure, not the object of evaluation. Use of internal data limits independent replication.

verdict_reason: Novel, practically important non-functional evaluation with a real fault-injection runtime and three frontier models, including industrial code. Caveats: custom oracles, no variance despite repeats, closed artifacts, possible contamination on OSS demos, and the skill's benefit is small and inconsistent.
applicability: Relevant to the delivery side: agent-written Java services will likely log a lot but not record dependency, timeout, retry and correlation-ID context needed to diagnose failures between services and downstream. Practical consequences: put observability requirements into the spec/acceptance criteria (which fields must be logged on dependency failure, timeouts, content-validation rejections), and check them deterministically (log-schema tests, fault-injection smoke tests in CI) rather than relying on an observability skill, which raised FSR by only 1-9 pp. Few-shot examples from the team's own repos helped more than generic 'add observability' prompts, so share a reference logging module across the several repositories. For domain content, the skill's 'avoid sensitive data' guidance matters but is unmeasured. Results are host-neutral (Copilot SDK harness) but per-language Java numbers are not given.
